question: to the Commission Tomáš Zdechovský (PPE) Subject:

Recent investigative reporting1 has revealed that Russian-linked ‘shadow airlines’ are allegedly operating from Algeria and conducting covert logistics missions, potentially circumventing EU sanctions and export controls. These activities raise serious concerns regarding the effectiveness of EU restrictive measures, the risk of dual-use goods being transferred, and the broader implications for the credibility of the EU’s security and foreign policy. At the same time, EU agencies such as Eurojust and bodies such as the European Public Prosecutor’s Office warn about the growing complexity and cross-border nature of organised crime and sanctions circumvention, while also facing increasing workloads and resource constraints. 1.
What concrete steps is the Commission taking to monitor and disrupt the use of non-EU hubs, such as Algeria, for the circumvention of EU sanctions by Russian-linked entities?
How does the Commission assess the role of ‘shadow aviation networks’ in facilitating sanctions evasion and potential transfers of dual-use or military-relevant goods?

Does the Commission intend to propose strengthening the mandates and resources of EU agencies and bodies (e.g. Europol, Eurojust and the European Public Prosecutor’s Office) to improve their capacity to investigate and prosecute increasingly sophisticated sanctions circumvention schemes?
https://www.defensenews.com/global/europe/2026/04/30/investigation-russian-shadow-airlines-usealgeria-as-base-for-secretive-missions/. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.7.2026) The Commission is aware of the operation of Russian state-affiliated aircraft flying into various third countries. Whilst these countries are not bound by EU sanctions, the EU Sanctions Envoy, David O’Sullivan, conducts diplomatic outreach to third countries identified as potential hubs for sanctions circumvention to find mutually agreeable solutions to avoid that EU sanctions are circumvented via these jurisdictions. The EU has also reinforced its anti-circumvention toolbox and has also imposed direct sanctions on companies based in third countries, that have been found to circumvent sanctions. The EU sanctions law also contains obligations on EU operators to ensure sanctioned goods are not supplied to Russia via third parties, such as deploying enhanced due diligence when trading in Common High Priority (CHP) items1 or inserting a ‘no re-export to Russia’ clause in their export contracts. EU agencies and bodies such as Europol, Eurojust and the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) are already competent to deal with sanctions violation cases, within their respective competences. Their role and cooperation have also been recognised in the Directive on the criminalisation of the violation of EU sanctions2. The Commission is taking due consideration of the reflections of a possible extension of the EPPO’s competence to sanctions violations in the context of the possible revision of the EPPO Regulation3, which the Commission may propose at the end of 2026. The Commission has also adopted a proposal for a revision of the Europol Regulation4 to equip the Agency with new capabilities to enhance its support to Member States’ investigations in targeting criminal assets owned by individuals and legal entities subject to EU sanctions.
